description:
Implement a last-in-first-out (LIFO) stack using only two queues. Support push(x), pop(), top(), and empty().

Allowed queue operations: add at the back, inspect or remove the front, read the size, and check whether it is empty. A list or deque may simulate a queue, but may only be used through these operations.

Constraints: values are integers from 1 to 9, with at most 100 method calls. Calls to pop() and top() always have an element available.

Follow-up: implement the same stack with just one queue. Both the two-queue solution and the one-queue follow-up are shown below.
intuition: A queue removes the oldest value first, while a stack needs the newest. Keep the newest value at the front of the active queue. To push, place the new value into an empty helper queue, then move all the older values behind it. Swap the queue roles so the helper becomes the active queue.
approach: Use an active queue and a helper queue. On push, enqueue the new value into the empty helper, transfer every active element from front to helper back, then swap the queues. The helper is empty again. Pop and top use the active queue’s front; empty checks its size.
jsWalkthrough:
Queue contents are shown front to back.

Start: active=[], helper=[]

push(1): enqueue 1 into helper -> helper=[1]
  Nothing to transfer. Swap -> active=[1], helper=[]

push(2): enqueue 2 into helper -> helper=[2]
  Transfer front 1 -> active=[], helper=[2,1]
  Swap -> active=[2,1], helper=[]

top(): return 2; active stays [2,1]
pop(): return 2; active becomes [1]
empty(): return false

Output: [null, null, null, 2, 2, false]
explanation:
1. Maintain two queues: active stores the stack order; helper starts empty.
2. Enqueue the new value into helper before transferring the old values behind it.
3. Dequeue each active front and enqueue it at helper’s back, preserving the old stack order.
4. Swap the queue references. The newest value is now at active’s front, and helper is empty.
5. Pop dequeues the active front; top peeks without removal; empty checks active’s size.
6. With O(1) queue operations, push transfers n existing elements and takes O(n); pop, top, and empty each take O(1).
timeComplexity: Constructor: O(1); push: O(n + 1); pop / top / empty: O(1)
hints: Keep the newest value at the front of the active queue.
Enqueue the new value into an empty helper before moving the old values into it.
After transferring all old values, swap the active and helper queue references.

followUp.title: One queue
followUp.approach: Replace the helper queue with rotation. Enqueue the new value, then move exactly size - 1 older values from front to back. The new value reaches the front, with the previous stack order behind it. Pop, top, and empty still use only standard queue operations.
followUp.jsWalkthrough:
Operations: push(1), push(2), top(), pop(), empty()

push(1):
  queue = [1]
  rotations = 1-1 = 0 -> no rotations
  queue = [1]

push(2):
  queue = [1, 2] after push
  rotations = 2-1 = 1
  Rotation 1: shift front=1, push to back -> queue=[2,1]
  queue = [2, 1] (newest element 2 is at front)

top():
  return queue[0] = 2

pop():
  return queue.shift() = 2
  queue = [1]

empty():
  queue.length = 1 -> return false

Output: [null, null, null, 2, 2, false]
followUp.explanation:
1. Solve the explicitly allowed one-queue follow-up using a deque in Python or an array in JavaScript.
2. On push: add element, then rotate all previous elements to the back.
3. This puts the newest element at the front (LIFO order).
4. Pop and top simply access the front of the queue.
5. With O(1) queue operations, rotating n existing elements makes push O(n).
6. Pop, top, and empty each use a single queue operation and take O(1).
followUp.timeComplexity: Constructor: O(1); push: O(n + 1); pop / top / empty: O(1)
